atomicClaims.statement: Men age 65 through 75 who have ever smoked should receive one-time abdominal ultrasound screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm.
atomicClaims.limitation: Exact pre-existing atomic statement and stable claim ID retained; source mapping freshly verified. Limited to asymptomatic previously unscreened men; not a diagnostic strategy for symptoms.
atomicClaims.applicablePopulation: Asymptomatic men 65-75 with previous tobacco use and no completed abdominal aortic screen.

atomicClaims.statement: An acceptable-risk patient with an asymptomatic 6-cm fusiform abdominal aortic aneurysm should receive prompt vascular-surgery evaluation for elective repair rather than routine surveillance alone.
atomicClaims.limitation: Exact pre-existing statement/ID retained. Anatomy, life expectancy and operative risk still govern final repair selection.
atomicClaims.applicablePopulation: Stable acceptable-risk men with intact fusiform AAA.

atomicClaims.statement: AAA size assessment includes the outer aneurysm wall, not just the contrast-filled lumen.
atomicClaims.limitation: CT measurements must be perpendicular to the aortic path. One directly checked society publication.

atomicClaims.statement: Growth assessment requires comparable landmarks and measurement planes.
atomicClaims.limitation: A single oblique axial value cannot establish growth against an orthogonal prior value; repeat measurement of existing images can resolve this without repeat acquisition.

atomicClaims.statement: For asymptomatic men with a 4.0-4.9-cm AAA, annual ultrasound surveillance is recommended.
atomicClaims.limitation: Not a policy for women, symptoms, rapid confirmed growth or poor ultrasound definition.
atomicClaims.applicablePopulation: Stable asymptomatic men with small fusiform AAA.

atomicClaims.statement: A 3.0-3.9-cm AAA can undergo ultrasound surveillance every three years.
atomicClaims.limitation: For asymptomatic disease without a separate concerning change.

atomicClaims.statement: Six-month ultrasound surveillance applies to unrepaired AAAs at least 5.0 cm in men or 4.5 cm in women.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single checked guideline; do not use surveillance to defer an otherwise indicated repair assessment.

atomicClaims.statement: For women with a 4.0-4.4-cm AAA, annual ultrasound surveillance is recommended.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single checked guideline; symptoms or other concerning findings can change the plan.

atomicClaims.statement: An intact AAA of at least 5.0 cm in a woman warrants elective repair assessment.
atomicClaims.limitation: Recommendation strength differs by society; diameter does not override operative fitness or preferences.

atomicClaims.statement: Symptoms attributable to an intact AAA warrant repair assessment regardless of usual asymptomatic diameter thresholds.
atomicClaims.limitation: Pain attribution requires clinical assessment; no universal numeric pain or observation interval is supplied.

atomicClaims.statement: Preserve at least one internal iliac inflow when feasible during aortoiliac repair.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single directly checked guideline; describes pelvic-perfusion protection, not a universal brand or device choice.
atomicClaims.applicablePopulation: AAA repair involving iliac landing zones.

atomicClaims.statement: Attachment-site flow into an excluded sac represents a sealing failure.
atomicClaims.limitation: Type I origin; one directly checked specialty standard.

atomicClaims.statement: An established type I endoleak warrants prompt correction of the seal.
atomicClaims.limitation: Cuff extension requires an available healthy landing segment; complex cases may need other repair. One directly checked publication.

atomicClaims.statement: Retrograde flow from aortic side branches can fill the excluded sac.
atomicClaims.limitation: Type II physiology; other inflow sources must be assessed.

atomicClaims.statement: An isolated type II endoleak with stable sac size can undergo imaging follow-up.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single publication; requires exclusion of higher-pressure leaks and continued surveillance.
atomicClaims.applicablePopulation: Asymptomatic patients with stable post-EVAR sac.

atomicClaims.statement: Sac enlargement with uncertain leak origin requires investigation for occult type I or III inflow.
atomicClaims.limitation: Catheter angiography with possible cone-beam CT can resolve inconclusive CTA; no disputed growth cutoff is taught.

atomicClaims.statement: Separated modular components can directly pressurize the excluded sac.
atomicClaims.limitation: Type IIIa mechanism; not retrograde branch flow.

atomicClaims.statement: A bridging graft can close a component gap causing a type III endoleak.
atomicClaims.limitation: Prompt repair is indicated; anatomy determines the precise device or need for open conversion. One checked publication.

atomicClaims.statement: A stable patient with suspected ruptured AAA can undergo urgent CT for repair planning.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single checked guideline; do not extend imaging delay to a patient who cannot remain stable.

atomicClaims.statement: EVAR is recommended for ruptured AAA when anatomy is suitable.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single checked guideline; requires specialist capability, access and device suitability, not diameter alone.

atomicClaims.statement: Ascending aortic involvement establishes type A dissection even with a distal entry tear.
atomicClaims.limitation: Classification depends on extent, not simply the tear location.

atomicClaims.statement: Acute type A dissection requires emergency surgical evaluation and immediate repair.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single checked multisociety guideline. This draft does not rank contested mesenteric-first strategies.

atomicClaims.statement: Uncomplicated acute type B dissection initially receives medical therapy and close monitoring.
atomicClaims.limitation: High-risk morphology and later complications can change the plan; does not ban elective later TEVAR.
atomicClaims.applicablePopulation: Acute descending dissection without rupture or malperfusion.

atomicClaims.statement: Use intravenous beta blockade first, adding intravenous vasodilation if pressure remains high.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single directly checked recommendation; contraindications can favor a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker. No dose or numeric target is authored.
atomicClaims.applicablePopulation: Hypertensive acute aortic syndrome without beta-blocker contraindication.

atomicClaims.statement: Acute type B dissection with organ malperfusion warrants intervention, commonly TEVAR when suitable.
atomicClaims.limitation: Static branch disease can require adjuncts; no automatic bowel resection or non-aneurysm ischemia objective is included.

atomicClaims.statement: Sealing a dissection entry can expand the true lumen and relieve dynamic branch obstruction.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single current specialty standard; response must be reassessed.

atomicClaims.statement: Persistent fixed branch narrowing after central true-lumen expansion may require branch stenting.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single specialty standard; the case supplies persistent gradient and flap extension rather than assuming every residual image needs treatment.

atomicClaims.statement: Planned left-subclavian coverage should account for a patent LIMA coronary graft by preserving its inflow.
atomicClaims.limitation: Elective setting with native landing zones; bypass versus transposition depends on anatomy.
atomicClaims.applicablePopulation: TEVAR involving LSA with LIMA-dependent myocardium.

atomicClaims.statement: Carotid-subclavian transposition requires temporary proximal subclavian clamping.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single directly checked guideline; the anatomy-specific interruption matters for a pedicled LIMA.

atomicClaims.statement: A patent pedicled LIMA coronary graft favors bypass over subclavian transposition to avoid interrupting coronary inflow.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single directly checked guideline, section on LSA revascularization; other bypass/endovascular configurations remain specialist decisions.
atomicClaims.applicablePopulation: LSA revascularization with a patent pedicled LIMA.

atomicClaims.statement: New spinal-cord dysfunction after TEVAR calls for perfusion rescue, including pressure support and CSF drainage assessment.
atomicClaims.limitation: Rapid specialist response; drainage contraindications must be checked. No invented target, timing, guaranteed recovery or routine prophylactic drain rule.

atomicClaims.statement: A small PAA with thrombus and distal embolic findings merits repair consideration despite being below 20 mm.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single guideline, weak recommendation/low-quality evidence; excludes acutely threatened limbs requiring an ischemia-specific pathway.
atomicClaims.applicablePopulation: PAA under 20 mm with embolic findings.

atomicClaims.statement: Finding a PAA warrants screening the opposite popliteal artery and abdominal aorta.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single guideline, strong recommendation/moderate evidence; this is aneurysm screening, not broad asymptomatic arterial-stenosis screening.

atomicClaims.statement: A symptomatic expanding excluded PAA sac may require decompression despite a patent bypass.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single guideline; exclude graft failure and venous thrombosis as the cause of symptoms.

atomicClaims.statement: Unexplained infection or gastrointestinal bleeding after aortic grafting warrants cross-sectional graft evaluation.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single guideline; imaging and cultures are interpreted together, and an unrevealing endoscopy does not assess the graft.
atomicClaims.applicablePopulation: Prosthetic aortic graft with unexplained infection/bleeding.

atomicClaims.statement: An operable stable patient with aortic graft infection can undergo graft source-control surgery and arterial reconstruction.
atomicClaims.limitation: Specific reconstruction and antimicrobial regimen need specialist judgment; endovascular bridging or suppression may fit other patients.

atomicClaims.statement: Open repair is preferred for an intact TAAA requiring repair in Marfan syndrome.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single directly checked guideline; does not preclude endovascular rescue or exceptional high-risk situations. Newer ESVS full text was inaccessible.
atomicClaims.applicablePopulation: Fit patient with heritable native-aorta TAAA.

atomicClaims.statement: Pancreatitis can disrupt an adjacent artery and produce a contained arterial leak.
atomicClaims.limitation: One CC BY specialty standard. The synthetic image observations are not a copied figure.

atomicClaims.statement: Visceral pseudoaneurysms generally warrant prompt treatment rather than true-aneurysm size surveillance.
atomicClaims.limitation: Single standard; small intraparenchymal lesions can be exceptions. This case is an extraparenchymal splenic-artery wall defect; exact true-aneurysm thresholds remain withheld.

explanation.text: An ever-smoker in the eligible age range still needs a first abdominal aortic screen when prior imaging covered the chest. Ultrasound is the initial screening modality.

choices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound
choices.rationale: He was an eligible previously unscreened man; chest imaging did not examine the abdominal aorta.
choices.temptation: Selects the recommended screening modality after checking prior coverage.
choices.counterfactual: An adequate previous abdominal aortic screen would remove the indication for a new one-time screen.

choices.label: Abdominal aortic CT angiography
choices.rationale: CTA can define repair anatomy but is not the routine first screen for this asymptomatic eligible man.
choices.temptation: Treats the greater anatomic detail of CTA as a reason to use it for screening.
choices.counterfactual: New pain with suspected symptomatic AAA would favor diagnostic CT rather than preventive ultrasound.

choices.label: No additional aortic imaging
choices.rationale: The previous study ended before the abdominal aorta, and remote smoking still counts as ever smoking.
choices.temptation: Counts any previous aortic scan or remote cessation as a completed screen.
choices.counterfactual: A documented adequate prior abdominal aortic screen could make no repeat one-time screening appropriate.

explanation.text: Use the full outer-wall aneurysm diameter. A stable acceptable-risk man with a 6-cm fusiform AAA needs elective vascular repair evaluation; mural thrombus does not reduce that diameter to the flowing channel.

choices.label: Refer for elective vascular repair evaluation
choices.rationale: Repair assessment uses the outer aneurysm diameter; the patent channel understates sac size.
choices.temptation: Recognizes that thrombus does not remove the surrounding sac from size assessment.
choices.counterfactual: A small stable full sac diameter would support surveillance instead.

choices.label: Arrange annual aortic ultrasound surveillance
choices.rationale: A 3.1-cm patent lumen is not the relevant aneurysm diameter; the full sac is 6.0 cm.
choices.temptation: Uses the smaller channel as the aneurysm measurement.
choices.counterfactual: A stable 4.7-cm full sac in an asymptomatic man would support annual ultrasound.

choices.label: Arrange three-year aortic ultrasound surveillance
choices.rationale: A surveillance schedule for a much smaller AAA is inappropriate for this full sac size.
choices.temptation: Treats thrombus as an exclusion of the aneurysmal wall and follows a small-AAA interval.
choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic 3.1-cm full aneurysm, rather than a 3.1-cm lumen inside a 6-cm sac, could support this interval.

explanation.text: Compare the same anatomic site with reproducible orthogonal measurements. Reformat the available acquisitions before labeling the difference as growth; repeating the scan is not necessary just to correct a measurement plane.

choices.label: Re-measure both CT datasets perpendicular to the centerline
choices.rationale: Different measurement planes can create an apparent increase; the acquired data permit a comparable assessment.
choices.temptation: Checks measurement validity before assigning growth.
choices.counterfactual: If matched orthogonal measurements confirmed enlargement, reassessment rather than another reformat would be needed.

choices.label: Acquire another contrast CT using the new axial protocol
choices.rationale: Another noncomparable acquisition does not resolve the existing plane mismatch.
choices.temptation: Mistakes measurement inconsistency for a need to repeat acquisition.
choices.counterfactual: An unavailable or technically inadequate existing acquisition could require new CT imaging.

choices.label: Replace the CT comparison with a new ultrasound diameter
choices.rationale: A new modality does not establish how the two existing CT measurements relate.
choices.temptation: Uses a third number to arbitrate a methodological discrepancy.
choices.counterfactual: Once a comparable small stable AAA is established, ultrasound is suitable for ongoing surveillance.

explanation.text: The matched study establishes a 4.7-cm AAA, not a confirmed jump to 5.3 cm. Annual ultrasound is the guideline schedule for an asymptomatic man in this diameter band when ultrasound defines the sac adequately.

choices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound every 12 months
choices.rationale: The matched size places this asymptomatic man in the annual-ultrasound group.
choices.temptation: Integrates comparable size, absence of symptoms and usable ultrasound.
choices.counterfactual: A larger diameter near the male repair threshold would shorten surveillance.

choices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound every 6 months
choices.rationale: This follows a larger-AAA schedule rather than the supported schedule for his matched 4.7-cm diameter.
choices.temptation: Uses the unreconciled 5.3-cm report or applies the female size bands to this man.
choices.counterfactual: A stable asymptomatic man with a 5.2-cm AAA could reasonably receive six-month surveillance.

choices.label: Abdominal aortic ultrasound every 3 years
choices.rationale: This is too long for the measured 4.7-cm sac.
choices.temptation: Applies a small-AAA surveillance interval to the wrong size band.
choices.counterfactual: A stable asymptomatic 3.5-cm AAA would support a three-year interval.

explanation.text: A symptomatic intact AAA is assessed for repair even below the usual asymptomatic diameter threshold. The new localized persistent pain changes the previous surveillance premise; hemodynamic stability and absence of a CT leak do not restore that premise.

choices.label: Inpatient vascular assessment for aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: The new pain pattern and localized findings support aneurysm-attributable symptoms despite a subthreshold asymptomatic diameter.
choices.temptation: Reassesses the earlier plan when the care phase changes.
choices.counterfactual: Reproducible mechanical pain with a separate established cause would support returning to size-based surveillance.

choices.label: Outpatient ultrasound surveillance in six months
choices.rationale: A shorter surveillance interval does not address the new symptomatic aneurysm assessment.
choices.temptation: Treats the earlier size-based plan as valid despite the new symptom evidence.
choices.counterfactual: A larger but asymptomatic unrepaired AAA can merit six-month follow-up.

choices.label: Outpatient ultrasound surveillance in twelve months
choices.rationale: The old annual plan was for an asymptomatic patient; the current observations change that premise.
choices.temptation: Anchors on the earlier node's correct annual interval.
choices.counterfactual: With an independently established nonaneurysmal pain cause and no AAA symptoms, annual surveillance of a stable 4.9-cm male AAA would be reasonable.

explanation.text: A stable diameter can still warrant repair evaluation. The guideline boundary is lower in women than men, but it does not prescribe a procedure or an individual mortality estimate.

choices.label: Elective vascular evaluation for aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: The size meets the female repair-assessment boundary even without interval growth.
choices.temptation: Uses the appropriate population and leaves the actual procedure to anatomic and operative assessment.
choices.counterfactual: A smaller asymptomatic sac would favor continued imaging surveillance.

choices.label: Aortic ultrasound surveillance every six months
choices.rationale: A male size band should not postpone this woman's repair assessment.
choices.temptation: Applies the male threshold and waits for growth to establish eligibility.
choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic woman with a 4.7-cm AAA could receive six-month surveillance.

choices.label: Aortic ultrasound surveillance every twelve months
choices.rationale: Annual follow-up does not address a woman's aneurysm already at the repair-assessment boundary.
choices.temptation: Assumes stability negates a size indication or applies the wrong surveillance band.
choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic woman with a 4.2-cm AAA could receive annual surveillance.

explanation.text: The left internal iliac artery is already occluded. Use a configuration that excludes the aneurysms while preserving the patent right pelvic inflow when feasible; landing within an aneurysmal common iliac segment does not solve exclusion.

choices.label: Right iliac branch graft; left external-iliac extension
choices.rationale: This preserves the patent right internal iliac route while excluding the aneurysmal common iliac segments.
choices.temptation: Maps inflow, outflow and the remaining pelvic circulation.
choices.counterfactual: If no right internal-iliac landing segment existed, a different reconstruction would need assessment.

choices.label: Bilateral external-iliac extensions; right internal-iliac embolization
choices.rationale: This would eliminate the remaining direct internal-iliac inflow when a preserving option is anatomically described.
choices.temptation: Prioritizes simple exclusion of both common iliac aneurysms without accounting for the contralateral occlusion.
choices.counterfactual: Loss of an internal-iliac artery can be acceptable when the other remains patent and preservation is not feasible.

choices.label: Bilateral limb landings within the distal common iliac arteries
choices.rationale: The proposed landing regions remain aneurysmal through the bifurcations and do not supply a healthy distal seal.
choices.temptation: Avoids internal-iliac interruption by retaining the usual common-iliac landing position.
choices.counterfactual: Nonaneurysmal common iliac landing segments could permit this configuration.

explanation.text: Delayed branch-associated flow with an unchanged sac supports continued surveillance. A visible leak is not enough to choose its treatment; source and sac behavior matter.

choices.label: Continue aortic duplex imaging surveillance
choices.rationale: The branch origin and unchanged sac support observation with continued imaging.
choices.temptation: Interprets both the leak route and sac behavior.
choices.counterfactual: A direct attachment leak or a growing sac would require a different evaluation or intervention.

choices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
choices.rationale: A visible branch leak does not by itself establish a treatment benefit when the sac is stable.
choices.temptation: Treats persistence of any contrast outside the graft as a repair indication.
choices.counterfactual: A persistent proven branch leak with consequential sac growth can merit embolization after other sources are excluded.

choices.label: Extend the proximal seal with an aortic cuff
choices.rationale: The observed inflow is from lumbar branches, not the proximal attachment.
choices.temptation: Confuses every leak with a proximal seal failure.
choices.counterfactual: A proximal attachment leak with a usable extra landing segment would favor cuff extension.

explanation.text: Do not carry forward a branch-leak label when a growing sac has an uncertain current inflow source. Problem-solving aortography can assess the attachments and modular junctions before choosing a branch-directed treatment.

choices.label: Aortography across the seal zones and graft junctions
choices.rationale: The enlarging sac and uncertain source require reassessment for direct graft or attachment inflow before targeting a branch.
choices.temptation: Questions whether the old branch label explains the current growth.
choices.counterfactual: A clearly established enlarging isolated branch leak could move directly to targeted branch mapping and embolization.

choices.label: Selective mesenteric-to-inferior-mesenteric collateral angiography
choices.rationale: This maps a branch route but does not resolve the possible attachment or component defect producing the current sac growth.
choices.temptation: Extends the previous type-II attribution to a new scan without validating it.
choices.counterfactual: Proven inferior-mesenteric branch inflow into a growing sac can justify this approach.

choices.label: Selective iliolumbar-to-lumbar collateral angiography
choices.rationale: The lumbar branch near the contrast focus does not establish that it is the only source.
choices.temptation: Anchors on the branch seen on the earlier surveillance images.
choices.counterfactual: A confirmed isolated lumbar leak with sac growth can be mapped for targeted embolization.

explanation.text: The direct component gap is a type III mechanism and requires prompt repair. A covered bridge across the separation closes the source; branch embolization or a remote proximal extension would not.

choices.label: Bridge the separated components with a covered graft
choices.rationale: The source is the modular gap; a bridging covered component restores continuity.
choices.temptation: Matches the repair to the observed mechanical failure.
choices.counterfactual: A branch-fed leak without component disruption would require a different strategy.

choices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
choices.rationale: Branch embolization does not close the direct connection through the separated graft components.
choices.temptation: Persists with the earlier lumbar explanation despite new central findings.
choices.counterfactual: A proven isolated growing lumbar leak can warrant embolization.

choices.label: Extend the proximal attachment with an aortic cuff
choices.rationale: The proximal seal is intact; extending it does not cover the limb junction gap.
choices.temptation: Recognizes a high-pressure leak but repairs the wrong level.
choices.counterfactual: A proximal attachment defect with additional landing length could be treated by a cuff.

explanation.text: This arterial-phase attachment route represents a type I sealing failure. Prompt seal repair is appropriate even before the sac enlarges; the available healthy neck makes proximal extension a supported option.

choices.label: Extend the proximal seal with an aortic cuff
choices.rationale: Direct attachment inflow requires prompt seal correction; the remaining healthy segment supports a cuff.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes a sealing defect from a stable branch leak.
choices.counterfactual: Absent a usable neck, a more complex reconstruction would need consideration.

choices.label: Continue aortic duplex imaging surveillance
choices.rationale: Stable sac size does not justify observation of an established late direct attachment leak.
choices.temptation: Overgeneralizes conservative care for stable type-II flow.
choices.counterfactual: A confirmed isolated branch leak with stable sac size supports surveillance.

choices.label: Embolize the lumbar inflow and sac cavity
choices.rationale: The demonstrated source is the proximal attachment, not a side branch.
choices.temptation: Treats contrast in the sac as a branch-leak problem regardless of its observed source.
choices.counterfactual: A growing isolated branch leak could support branch/sac embolization.

explanation.text: At the recorded stable assessment, urgent CT supplies cross-sectional repair-planning anatomy in suspected rupture rather than repeating the already demonstrated aneurysm diameter.

choices.label: CT angiography of the aorta and iliac access vessels
choices.rationale: Urgent CT can identify contained rupture and the anatomy needed for the repair strategy while he remains stable.
choices.temptation: Uses current physiology and the information required for repair, rather than repeating aneurysm detection.
choices.counterfactual: A patient unable to sustain circulation for imaging would need immediate hemorrhage-control decisions.

choices.label: Duplex ultrasound of the abdominal aorta and iliac vessels
choices.rationale: Another sonographic survey does not provide the same cross-sectional rupture and repair-planning information.
choices.temptation: Extends the correct screening modality to a suspected-rupture planning problem.
choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic small AAA being surveilled is appropriately assessed by ultrasound.

choices.label: Catheter aortography of the infrarenal aorta and iliac vessels
choices.rationale: Initial catheter luminal imaging does not replace CT mapping of the sac, surrounding hemorrhage and access anatomy in this stable setting.
choices.temptation: Treats proximity to an endovascular procedure as a reason to skip cross-sectional planning.
choices.counterfactual: Catheter angiography is useful during an intervention or for an unresolved post-EVAR leak source.

explanation.text: The wall defect and contiguous hematoma establish rupture. Preserved pressure does not make it elective. With documented suitable anatomy and treating-hospital expertise, the guideline favors emergency EVAR over open repair.

choices.label: Emergency endovascular aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: The record demonstrates rupture and device-suitable anatomy; guideline recommendations favor EVAR in that setting.
choices.temptation: Recognizes containment as rupture rather than a reason to delay and uses the documented anatomic suitability.
choices.counterfactual: An unsuitable proximal seal or access anatomy could favor open repair instead.

choices.label: Emergency open aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: Open repair is a real alternative, but the guideline favors EVAR for the documented suitable anatomy.
choices.temptation: Treats rupture as an automatic indication for open exposure.
choices.counterfactual: Inability to achieve an endovascular seal or obtain access could make open repair the appropriate choice.

choices.label: Elective endovascular aneurysm repair
choices.rationale: The wall defect and retroperitoneal hematoma establish rupture despite current preserved pressure.
choices.temptation: Misinterprets containment and stable circulation as an intact elective aneurysm.
choices.counterfactual: An intact asymptomatic qualifying aneurysm could undergo elective repair planning.

explanation.text: Ascending involvement determines the type-A pathway even when the entry tear is distal. Stable current pressure does not remove the need for emergency surgical treatment of acute ascending dissection.

choices.label: Emergency open ascending aortic repair
choices.rationale: Ascending involvement places this in the type-A pathway despite a descending entry tear.
choices.temptation: Classifies by the involved segment and applies its urgent surgical consequence.
choices.counterfactual: A flap confined distal to the left subclavian without complications would favor initial medical treatment.

choices.label: Urgent descending thoracic endovascular repair
choices.rationale: Treating the distal tear as a type-B problem does not address the acute ascending involvement.
choices.temptation: Classifies the dissection by the tear location alone.
choices.counterfactual: A complicated dissection confined to the descending aorta with suitable anatomy can favor TEVAR.

choices.label: Intravenous esmolol with CT angiographic follow-up
choices.rationale: Impulse control is background stabilization but not definitive treatment of acute ascending dissection.
choices.temptation: Uses normotension and absence of malperfusion to choose an uncomplicated type-B pathway.
choices.counterfactual: An uncomplicated dissection confined to the descending aorta initially receives medical therapy and monitoring.

explanation.text: The initial record shows descending dissection with preserved organ perfusion and no rupture. Start monitored medical impulse control. Intravenous beta blockade comes before additional vasodilation when pressure remains high and beta blockade is not contraindicated.

choices.label: Intravenous esmolol, then nicardipine if pressure remains high
choices.rationale: The observed extent and perfusion support initial medical treatment; rate/impulse control precedes added vasodilation.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes initial hypertension from persistent complications despite adequate treatment.
choices.counterfactual: New organ malperfusion despite treatment would change the need for intervention.

choices.label: Urgent thoracic endovascular stent-graft repair
choices.rationale: The admission record has not demonstrated rupture, malperfusion or failure of medical treatment that would establish an immediate repair indication.
choices.temptation: Treats every acute dissection or first elevated pressure as complicated disease.
choices.counterfactual: A suitable type-B dissection with new organ malperfusion generally warrants intervention.

choices.label: Urgent open descending aortic graft replacement
choices.rationale: An open replacement is not the initial treatment for this uncomplicated descending presentation.
choices.temptation: Overextends the acute ascending-dissection operation rule to a different extent and physiology.
choices.counterfactual: Complicated disease unsuitable for endovascular treatment can require open reconstruction.

explanation.text: Improved pressure and pain do not negate new organ malperfusion. The functional and CTA changes warrant intervention; TEVAR can relieve central dynamic true-lumen compression, after which branch perfusion must be reassessed.

choices.label: TEVAR with reassessment of renal perfusion
choices.rationale: The combination of functional decline and new inflow compromise demonstrates a complication requiring intervention, with residual branch flow reassessed after entry sealing.
choices.temptation: Uses organ trajectory rather than the improved pain or blood pressure as the endpoint.
choices.counterfactual: Preserved renal perfusion and function would support continued medical monitoring.

choices.label: Continue impulse infusions with renal observation
choices.rationale: Achieved pressure control does not resolve the new structural inflow compromise and renal deterioration.
choices.temptation: Attributes the creatinine change to treatment or contrast and remains anchored on an initially uncomplicated course.
choices.counterfactual: An uncomplicated course without malperfusion can continue monitored medical therapy.

choices.label: Open descending replacement with renal reassessment
choices.rationale: Open repair is a real treatment, but documented TEVAR suitability supports the less invasive central repair strategy in this setting.
choices.temptation: Correctly escalates care but treats all organ malperfusion as requiring open aortic exposure.
choices.counterfactual: Unsuitable sealing/access anatomy or relevant heritable disease could shift toward open repair.

explanation.text: The response separates mechanisms: central true-lumen compression improved, but a fixed flap within the renal artery still limits perfusion. Branch stenting can treat that static lesion rather than repeating a successful central repair.

choices.label: Stent the obstructed left renal artery segment
choices.rationale: The central problem has improved, but a fixed dissected branch lesion continues to impede perfusion.
choices.temptation: Localizes the residual obstruction after observing the central repair response.
choices.counterfactual: If branch flow recovered after central true-lumen expansion, an additional renal stent would not follow from these findings.

choices.label: Fenestrate the distal aortic dissection septum
choices.rationale: This targets a persistent central dynamic pressure problem, whereas the demonstrated residual defect is fixed within the branch.
choices.temptation: Carries forward the original dynamic-compression mechanism despite the documented response.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent dynamic aortic flap-related obstruction after entry treatment can merit fenestration.

choices.label: Extend the thoracic graft over the proximal seal
choices.rationale: The entry is sealed and central true-lumen expansion has already occurred; a proximal extension does not treat the fixed renal segment.
choices.temptation: Assumes every perfusion failure after TEVAR reflects inadequate central sealing.
choices.counterfactual: An incompletely sealed entry with persistent central compression could require graft revision.

explanation.text: Protect the pedicled LIMA coronary inflow before elective LSA coverage. Bypass avoids the proximal subclavian clamp required for transposition; waiting for arm ischemia also fails to protect this coronary-dependent territory.

choices.label: Carotid-subclavian bypass before aortic coverage
choices.rationale: LSA interruption threatens inflow to the patent LIMA graft supplying an occluded native LAD territory.
choices.temptation: Follows the coronary conduit back to its inflow origin.
choices.counterfactual: If no LSA-dependent coronary or other critical inflow existed, timing and need could differ, particularly in an emergency.

choices.label: Aortic coverage, then bypass if arm ischemia develops
choices.rationale: An arm-symptom trigger does not protect the LIMA-dependent coronary circulation during elective coverage.
choices.temptation: Treats upper-extremity symptoms as the only meaningful consequence of LSA interruption.
choices.counterfactual: Selective delayed revascularization may fit some emergency coverings without critical LSA-dependent inflow.

choices.label: Carotid-subclavian transposition before aortic coverage
choices.rationale: Transposition requires proximal subclavian clamping, which can interrupt the patent pedicled LIMA coronary inflow; bypass avoids that required interruption.
choices.temptation: Chooses a durable LSA revascularization while overlooking its proximal clamp sequence.
choices.counterfactual: Without a patent pedicled LIMA or another clamp-dependent inflow, transposition can be a reasonable LSA revascularization technique.

explanation.text: Bilateral leg weakness after hypotension with preserved limb pulses raises concern for spinal-cord ischemia. Activate perfusion rescue and specialist CSF-drainage assessment; the new phase calls for restoring cord perfusion rather than intensifying impulse reduction.

choices.label: Vasopressor-supported perfusion with CSF-drainage rescue
choices.rationale: The pattern points to spinal-cord perfusion injury; pressure support and reduction of intrathecal pressure address that mechanism.
choices.temptation: Links bilateral motor findings with the hypotensive trigger and preserved limb inflow.
choices.counterfactual: A focal cerebral syndrome or arterial inflow loss would require a different rescue target.

choices.label: Esmolol-based pressure reduction with intravenous analgesia
choices.rationale: Further pressure reduction would work against perfusion rescue in this new postoperative neurologic syndrome.
choices.temptation: Carries an acute aortic impulse-reduction plan into a phase where low pressure is the precipitating problem.
choices.counterfactual: An unrepaired hypertensive acute aortic syndrome without cord hypoperfusion supports impulse control.

choices.label: Heparin anticoagulation with urgent aortoiliac thrombectomy
choices.rationale: Warm feet and preserved pulses make aortoiliac occlusion a poorer explanation than spinal perfusion injury.
choices.temptation: Interprets leg weakness after endovascular repair as an access or limb-occlusion complication.
choices.counterfactual: Sudden cold pulseless legs with demonstrated aortoiliac occlusion could require this pathway.

explanation.text: The relevant problem is distal embolization from a thrombus-containing PAA, not diameter alone. Repair is considered even below 20 mm when embolic complications are present; the exact operation still depends on operative assessment and conduit anatomy.

choices.label: Plan popliteal aneurysm exclusion and bypass
choices.rationale: The thrombus and distal embolic findings make size-only observation inadequate despite a diameter below 20 mm.
choices.temptation: Recognizes the symptomatic source while preserving the distinction from a threatened limb emergency.
choices.counterfactual: A small asymptomatic lesion without thrombus or poor runoff could remain under surveillance.

choices.label: Arrange annual popliteal duplex surveillance
choices.rationale: A diameter-only policy overlooks the repeated embolic complications documented here.
choices.temptation: Applies the usual asymptomatic small-PAA pathway to a symptomatic source.
choices.counterfactual: A small asymptomatic PAA without thrombus or embolic findings can be monitored.

choices.label: Begin anticoagulation with popliteal duplex follow-up
choices.rationale: Medical suppression does not remove the aneurysmal thrombus source; the supported next strategy includes repair consideration.
choices.temptation: Treats the embolic event without addressing its persistent source.
choices.counterfactual: A patient in whom repair must be deferred for prohibitive risk may require an interim specialist-directed medical plan.

explanation.text: PAA prompts an opposite-leg and abdominal-aortic aneurysm survey. Review what was actually acquired: a complete abdominal CTA already evaluates the aorta, but a right-leg-only duplex does not evaluate the left popliteal artery.

choices.label: Left popliteal arterial duplex ultrasound
choices.rationale: The abdominal aorta has been assessed, while the associated contralateral popliteal site is outside the documented unilateral acquisition.
choices.temptation: Combines the PAA association with the actual tested territory.
choices.counterfactual: If the left popliteal artery were already imaged adequately and the aorta were not, an abdominal aortic study would be appropriate.

choices.label: Repeat abdominal aortic duplex ultrasound
choices.rationale: The complete adequate abdominal CTA already addresses the aortic component of the associated-aneurysm survey.
choices.temptation: Recalls the AAA association but ignores the existing acquisition's scope.
choices.counterfactual: An incomplete abdominal assessment would support a dedicated aortic study.

choices.label: Thoracic aortic CT angiography
choices.rationale: The specific routinely recommended associated sites are the opposite popliteal artery and abdominal aorta, not a substitute thoracic survey.
choices.temptation: Generalizes aneurysm association into an unrestricted whole-arterial imaging search.
choices.counterfactual: An independent thoracic aneurysm or heritable-aortopathy indication could justify thoracic imaging.

explanation.text: A patent bypass does not remove an enlarging excluded sac. When that sac causes neural or venous compression, surgical decompression addresses the current problem rather than revising a patent conduit.

choices.label: Surgical decompression of the excluded aneurysm sac
choices.rationale: The symptomatic enlarging sac is the compressive target even though bypass inflow and outflow remain patent.
choices.temptation: Separates revascularization success from continued local aneurysm effects.
choices.counterfactual: An asymptomatic stable excluded sac would not establish a decompression indication.

choices.label: Revision of the popliteal bypass graft
choices.rationale: The bypass is patent; revising it does not remove the compressive sac.
choices.temptation: Treats new postoperative limb symptoms as graft failure.
choices.counterfactual: A demonstrated flow-limiting graft stenosis or occlusion could require revision.

choices.label: Embolization of residual genicular branch inflow
choices.rationale: Inflows can contribute to sac persistence, but the demonstrated symptomatic compression calls for decompression of the enlarged sac.
choices.temptation: Focuses on recurrent sac flow while overlooking the current compressive effect.
choices.counterfactual: Residual flow without symptomatic mass effect can prompt assessment of an inflow-directed strategy.

explanation.text: Infection or unexplained gastrointestinal bleeding after aortic grafting raises concern for a graft complication. Cross-sectional imaging evaluates the graft and surrounding bowel; a proximal endoscopic examination does not establish that this interface is normal.

choices.label: CT angiography of the aortic graft and adjacent bowel
choices.rationale: The graft history plus infection and bleeding warrants cross-sectional assessment of the reconstructed aorta and its bowel interface.
choices.temptation: Does not treat a negative proximal endoscopy as exclusion of a graft complication.
choices.counterfactual: A directly demonstrated ordinary mucosal bleeding lesion without graft-related findings could redirect the workup.

choices.label: Repeat upper endoscopy through the proximal duodenum
choices.rationale: Repeating the same examined mucosal territory does not evaluate the prosthetic graft or its extraluminal interface.
choices.temptation: Anchors on melena as necessarily a lesion within the already examined lumen.
choices.counterfactual: Recurrent bleeding from a known treatable proximal mucosal lesion could warrant repeat endoscopy.

choices.label: Tagged-red-cell scintigraphy for gastrointestinal bleeding
choices.rationale: Bleed localization does not assess the graft infection concern raised by the combined history and cultures.
choices.temptation: Seeks the intermittent bleeding site while treating bacteremia as an unrelated problem.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent intermittent bleeding after graft pathology has been excluded may need a separate bleeding-localization strategy.

explanation.text: Definitive surgery addresses infected prosthetic material and the bowel communication in an operable patient. Endovascular bridging and suppressive antibiotics have roles in other risk/instability settings; they do not establish equivalent source control here.

choices.label: Graft removal with arterial and bowel reconstruction
choices.rationale: The operable stable patient has an infected prosthesis with bowel communication; definitive surgery addresses the infected material and communication.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes definitive source control from bridging or suppression.
choices.counterfactual: Prohibitive operative risk could change the balance toward nonoperative suppression or a limited strategy.

choices.label: Covered endovascular relining across the affected graft
choices.rationale: Relining can bridge hemorrhage in instability or serve selected patients unsuitable for open surgery, but it leaves the infected prosthesis and bowel communication.
choices.temptation: Uses rapid bleeding control as though it establishes durable infection source control.
choices.counterfactual: Uncontrolled hemorrhage in an unstable patient can make an endovascular bridge reasonable.

choices.label: Retained graft with prolonged suppressive antimicrobial therapy
choices.rationale: Suppression does not remove the demonstrated source in this patient who can undergo definitive reconstruction.
choices.temptation: Equates a temporary physiologic response to antibiotics with eradication of an infected prosthesis.
choices.counterfactual: A patient who cannot tolerate reconstruction may need a suppression-based strategy after specialist review.

explanation.text: For an intact TAAA requiring repair in Marfan syndrome, the checked multisociety guideline favors open repair. Native-aortic tissue disease and long-term durability matter even when branched or hybrid reconstruction is technically possible.

choices.label: Open thoracoabdominal graft replacement
choices.rationale: Heritable native-aorta disease in an operable patient favors open reconstruction when repair is required.
choices.temptation: Distinguishes the tissue disease from an ordinary degenerative aneurysm.
choices.counterfactual: Severe operative prohibitions or emergency bridging needs can change the balance.

choices.label: Branched endovascular thoracoabdominal repair
choices.rationale: Technical feasibility does not erase the guideline preference for open repair in this heritable native-aorta setting.
choices.temptation: Generalizes the lower initial invasiveness of endovascular repair to all aneurysm substrates.
choices.counterfactual: An appropriate degenerative TAAA patient with higher open risk may be considered for branched repair.

choices.label: Visceral debranching with thoracic endografting
choices.rationale: A hybrid operation still relies on endograft sealing in the diseased native aorta rather than providing the preferred open reconstruction.
choices.temptation: Assumes adding open visceral bypasses resolves the native-seal concern.
choices.counterfactual: Selected patients unsuitable for conventional open repair can require alternative hybrid strategies.

explanation.text: A newly acquired cavity communicating through an arterial wall defect after pancreatitis supports a pseudoaneurysm mechanism. Its extra-organ location and wall disruption favor prompt vascular treatment assessment, despite small diameter and current stability.

choices.label: Prompt splenic-artery embolization assessment
choices.rationale: A new extra-organ contained leak through a wall defect is not governed by small true-aneurysm surveillance thresholds.
choices.temptation: Integrates the acquired wall defect and inflammatory setting with the rupture-risk management boundary.
choices.counterfactual: A small stable true aneurysm without symptoms can require a different surveillance decision.

choices.label: CT angiographic surveillance after inflammation resolves
choices.rationale: Waiting for inflammatory resolution leaves the demonstrated arterial wall defect unaddressed.
choices.temptation: Treats the cavity as a transient inflammatory change that can be reassessed with the collection.
choices.counterfactual: Selected small intraparenchymal pseudoaneurysms may be observed only under strict specialist follow-up; this is not that anatomy.

choices.label: Annual CT angiographic surveillance of lesion size
choices.rationale: A diameter-only true-aneurysm policy does not apply to an acquired extra-organ wall disruption.
choices.temptation: Lets the small 12-mm diameter override the lesion's mechanism.
choices.counterfactual: A stable small true visceral aneurysm in an appropriate patient may be surveilled after specialist assessment.
